The engineering context
CML3112, Week 3, slide 4

Explanation to give
Use a room or floor as the physical reference. Length and width are distances in metres. Multiplying them produces area in m²; multiplying by thickness produces volume in m³.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer

Start with numbers and values
CML3112, Week 3, slide 5

Explanation to give
Begin with a physical quantity: how many objects, or how much length? A number is the amount; a unit says what that amount measures. Python stores the number but does not automatically know the engineering unit.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Put 3 bolts beside 3 metres on the board. Both use the number 3, but adding them would make no physical sense. A length of 2.5 m is two whole metres plus half a metre.

Misconception to address
A decimal point does not supply a unit. Read the variable suffix, axis label or task definition before calculating.

On this slide
Number: A number expresses how much or how many: 3 items or 2.5 metres. Whole numbers count; decimal numbers can describe a part of a unit.
Value and unit: A value is one piece of information. The number 2.5 is a value. A measurement also needs a unit, such as metres. Python does not attach that unit automatically.

Explanation to give
Explain assignment as evaluating the right side and attaching the name on the left to that result. The name can later refer to a different value. Read the equals sign as “assign”, rather than as a mathematical claim that lasts forever.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
length_m = 4 makes length_m refer to 4. length_m = 6 replaces that association. Printing length_m now displays 6; the name does not remember a history of both values.

Misconception to address
Changing text in a notebook cell changes the instructions. The runtime value changes only when that cell executes.

On this slide
Variable: A name referring to a value. In length_m = 5, the right side is evaluated and assigned to length_m.
int, float, str, bool: int represents whole numbers; float represents approximate real numbers such as 2.5; str is text in quotes; bool is True or False.

Python values have types

Python values have types
CML3112, Week 3, slide 8

Explanation to give
Explain a type as the kind of information and the operations allowed on it. Quotes make a string, even when every character is a digit. int is a whole number; float is an approximation used for decimal-valued calculations; bool is a truth value.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
4 + 5 produces 9. "4" + "5" produces the text "45". int("4") + int("5") produces 9 because conversion occurs before addition. None represents the absence of a result in our examples.

Misconception to address
int("2.5") is invalid integer text. float("2.5") works. Converting a value is a deliberate action, not something Python always guesses.

On this slide
Type | Example | Meaning
int | 3 | Whole number
float | 3.5 | Decimal approximation
str | "3.5" | Text in quotes
bool | True / False | Logical value
NoneType | None | No value supplied
3.5 + 2 gives 5.5. "3.5" + "2" joins text into "3.52".

Explanation to give
Translate the familiar written arithmetic signs into keyboard characters. Addition and subtraction look familiar; multiplication uses * and division uses /. Explain each operation on two small numbers before discussing variables.

CML3112, Week 3, slide 10

Explanation to give
A function call asks an existing tool to do a job. Read its name first, then the values between parentheses. The comma separates inputs when more than one is supplied. The returned result can become input to another call.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
In print(float("4.5")), the inner float call converts text to 4.5, then print displays it. In print("length", 4), print receives two inputs and normally separates them with a space.

Misconception to address

On this slide
A built-in function: Python already provides tools such as print, type and float. A function call asks a named tool to do its work: print(3) displays 3.
Parentheses, quotes and comments: Parentheses hold the inputs to a call. Quotes make text: "3.5" is text; float("3.5") converts it to a number. # starts a comment that Python does not run.

Floor division remainder and powers

Floor division remainder and powers
CML3112, Week 3, slide 17

Explanation to give
Explain // as taking the floor of a quotient, % as the remainder and ** as repeated multiplication for a positive integer exponent. “Floor” means the greatest integer no larger than the quotient.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
9 = 2 × 4 + 1, so 9 // 4 is 2 and 9 % 4 is 1. 3 ** 2 is 9. For a negative example, -9 / 4 is -2.25, so -9 // 4 is -3.

Misconception to address
% does not mean percentage. To turn 60% into a fraction, use 60 / 100. Negative floor division does not simply remove the decimal digits.

On this slide
Operator | Meaning | Example and result
// | Floor the quotient | 7 // 2 gives 3
% | Remainder | 7 % 2 gives 1
** | Raise to a power | 2 ** 3 gives 8
7 contains three groups of 2 with 1 left over: 7 = 3 × 2 + 1.

Which operation happens first

Which operation happens first
CML3112, Week 3, slide 20

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Misconception to address
Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

On this slide
Parentheses group a calculation: do (2 + 3) before multiplying it by 4.

Powers come before multiplication and division. Multiplication, /, // and % come before addition and subtraction. Equal-level * and / run left to right.

Use parentheses when the intended grouping might be unclear. For a negative base, write (-2) ** 2. This gives 4; -(2 ** 2) gives -4.

https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html;

Assigning and updating a named value
CML3112, Week 3, slide 23

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

On this slide
count = 2 gives the name count the value 2. = means assignment; it does not ask whether two values are equal.

count = count + 1 first reads the old value 2, calculates 3, then assigns 3 back to count.

After the update, print(count) displays 3. Re-running only the update cell changes count again; restart and run from the beginning for the shown result.

CML3112, Week 3, slide 27

Explanation to give
Work from grouped subexpressions outward. Powers precede multiplication and division, which precede addition and subtraction. At the same multiplication/division level, work left to right.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
2 + 3 * 4 becomes 2 + 12 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 becomes 5 * 4 = 20. 12 / 3 * 2 becomes 4.0 * 2 = 8.0.

Parentheses can change the meaning. For a negative base, (-2) ** 2 is 4, while -(2 ** 2) is -4. Use a tolerance for approximate decimal results.

Many decimal fractions are approximate in a computer. A tolerance is an allowed difference, for example 0.01 m when checking two calculated lengths.

CML3112, Week 4, slide 14

Explanation to give
Read the right-hand occurrence of the name as its old value. Calculate the new value, then replace the old association. This is why an update works in programming even though count = count + 1 is not an algebraic equality.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
Start at count = 2. The update computes 2 + 1 and count becomes 3. Another execution of the update gives 4. Re-executing the initialisation first returns the sequence to 2, then 3.

Misconception to address
Initialise a running counter before the loop. Resetting it inside the loop throws away earlier progress.

On this slide
A counter records how many times an event happens. Set count = 0 before the loop, then count = count + 1 inside it.

count += 1 is a shorter spelling for that numeric update. Similarly, total += reading means total = total + reading.

The initial value belongs outside the loop. Resetting count to zero inside every iteration loses the earlier count.

A while loop checks before each repetition

A while loop checks before each repetition
CML3112, Week 4, slide 25

Explanation to give
while tests a condition before each iteration. Unlike for over a fixed list, it needs a route that eventually makes the condition False. Trace both the test and the state update.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
With count = 0 and while count < 3, print then increment yields 0, 1 and 2. The next test sees count 3 and stops before printing it.

Misconception to address
If count is never updated, the condition stays True. Interrupt a stuck runtime rather than waiting indefinitely, then identify the missing update.

On this slide
while count < 3: tests the condition before entering its indented block. True enters the block; False skips it and continues after the loop.

At the end of the body, return to the condition and test again. Unlike for, while does not automatically move to the next list item.

Something must make the condition become False, or the loop may continue indefinitely. In our example, count increases on every iteration.

Choosing if for or while

Choosing if for or while
CML3112, Week 4, slide 29

Explanation to give
if makes a decision once, for visits members of a collection, and while repeats while a condition remains True. Choose the construct by the job before writing syntax.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For three recorded temperatures, for visits all three. Inside it, if reading > 30 decides whether to count that observation. while is appropriate when repetition depends on a changing condition.

Misconception to address
A loop and a condition can appear together. They answer different questions: how often to repeat, and whether this item qualifies.

On this slide
Construct | Purpose | When it finishes
if / else | Choose a path once | After the chosen block
for | Visit supplied items | When items are exhausted
while | Repeat while True | When condition becomes False
A condition alone does not imply repetition: if tests once; while tests again after its body.

CML3112, Week 4, slide 30

Explanation to give
range supplies integers in order. Its stop value is excluded. Say the sequence out loud before executing the loop so the boundary is visible.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
range(3) supplies 0, 1, 2. range(1, 4) supplies 1, 2, 3. Both provide three integers but different starting points.

Misconception to address
The stop value itself is not visited. range counts steps and does not automatically retrieve values from a separate list.

On this slide

Precision / Recall

Precision / Recall
CML3113, Week 9, slide 11

Explanation to give
Use two different denominators. Precision looks only at issued warnings. Recall looks only at real cases that needed a warning. Say the population in the denominator before calculating.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
If TP=3, FP=1 and FN=2, precision is 3/(3+1)=0.75 and recall is 3/(3+2)=0.60. One asks whether warnings are reliable; the other asks whether true problems were found.

Misconception to address
The denominators are not interchangeable. Follow the published convention when a denominator is zero and explain why that case arises.

On this slide
Precision: Of all predicted warnings, the fraction that were actual warnings: TP / (TP + FP).
Recall: Of all actual warnings, the fraction detected: TP / (TP + FN).

Probability and a decision threshold

Probability and a decision threshold
CML3113, Week 9, slide 13

Explanation to give
A probability-like score becomes a class decision only after choosing a threshold. The threshold expresses an operating trade-off; an error-cost rule states which mistakes matter more for this task.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
At threshold >= 0.6, scores 0.59 and 0.60 give 0 and 1. Lowering the threshold usually raises more warnings, potentially reducing misses while increasing false alarms.

Misconception to address
A score of 0.8 is not a guarantee that this particular prediction is right. Evaluate calibration if probabilities will be interpreted literally. Costs must come from the stated scenario.

On this slide
Probability: A probability is between 0 and 1. Multiply by 100 for percent: 0.7 is 70%. A model’s probability is an estimate that needs checking.
Threshold: A threshold turns a score into a decision. For a rule score >= 0.5, a score of 0.7 gives class 1. Use validation data to choose the threshold.

Represent a category with indicators
CML3113, Week 9, slide 26

Explanation to give
One-hot encoding gives each category its own indicator column. A row has a 1 in the column matching its category and 0 in the others.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
For categories A and B, an A row becomes [1,0] and a B row becomes [0,1]. Assigning A=1 and B=2 could accidentally suggest a meaningful numerical distance or order.

Misconception to address
Fit the encoder on training data and define how to handle categories not seen during training. Do not invent an ordinal meaning for names.

On this slide
Category: A category is a label such as steel or timber. Its name does not imply a numerical size or rank.
One-hot indicator: Create a column for each category. Its entry is 1 when the row has that category and 0 otherwise. Learn the allowed categories from training data.

Accuracy can hide missed warnings

Accuracy can hide missed warnings
CML3113, Week 9, slide 28

Explanation to give
Accuracy counts all correct classifications together. In an imbalanced dataset, correct majority-class answers can dominate the score while the minority class is consistently missed.

Worked illustration / lecturer answer
With 95 normal cases and 5 genuine faults, always predicting normal gives 95% accuracy but detects zero faults. Fault recall is zero.

Misconception to address
A high headline accuracy alone is insufficient for a warning system. Report the confusion counts and the relevant costs.

On this slide
Accuracy = number of correct labels / number of labels. It counts correct warnings and correct non-warnings together.

If 90 of 100 cases need no warning, predicting no warning every time gives 90% accuracy. It detects none of the 10 real warnings: recall is 0.

Always inspect the actual/predicted counts and relevant costs before calling a classifier useful.

On this slide
Current I is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). Resistance R opposes that flow, measured in ohms.

Power P is energy transferred per second, measured in watts (W). Resistive heating follows P = I²R in this example.

I² means I × I. With I = 2 A and R = 3 ohms, P = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 W. This relationship motivates a feature; evaluation still tests whether it helps.
